Two new three-dimensional frameworks with zeolite-like channels have been prepared in the presence of 1,6-diaminohexane. title: 2610.0055v1
content_preview: Estimating moment or kshana as a lowest quantum time interval using the Heisenberg uncertainty relation, within the context of Compton effect and Fourier relationships for free wave packets. Shesharao M. Wanjerkhede 12 Oct. 2026 Abstract In this treatment, kshana or moment is used as a proposed lowest indivisible quantum of time, distinct from its philosophical origin and evaluated here as a physical hypothesis. Applying the Heisenberg uncertainty relation to particle localization through high-energy photon scattering in the Compton-effect framework, and Fourier relationships of free wave-packets estimated the lowest quantum time interval kshana or moment based on the statement of Maharishi Vyasa in his commentary on Patanjal Yog Darshan. The calculated lowest mean interval is ∆tmin = 1.93213300126795 × 10−21 sec, which is 4.5 % lower than the previously reported value 2.0233249470 ×10−21 sec, by the author. The value obtained from the Fourier relationships of free wave packets may be proposed as a lowest, indivisible quantum time kshana derived from the Heisenberg’s uncertainty relation. This discrepancy may arise from the uncertainty relation itself; however, the difference between two values, one from uncertainty relation and the other value found previously by the author requires further investigation. Results should therefore be read as a theoretical estimate dependent on the chosen uncertainty relation and localization assumptions, and the discrepancy with earlier values requires further mathematical and experimental scrutiny. Kshana is experimentally measurable in future. There are possibilities of using it for time measurement at subatomic level in physical science that studies matter, energy, and the fundamental laws of nature. title: nucleon
content_preview: The Electric Charge and Magnetization Distribution of the Nucleon: Evidence of a Subatomic Turing Wave Pattern Paul A. LaViolette, Ph.D. © February 22, 2008 The Starburst Foundation, 1176 Hedgewood Lane, Niskayuna, NY 12309 Electronic address: gravitics1@aol.com Published in: International Journal of General Systems, vol. 37 (6) (2008): 649-676. Abstract Subquantum kinetics, a physics methodology that applies general systems theoretic concepts to the field of microphysics has gained the status of being a viable unified field theory. Earlier publications of this theory had proposed that a subatomic particle should consist of an electrostatic field that has the form of a radial Turing wave pattern whose form is maintained through the ongoing activity of a nonlinear reaction-diffusion medium that fills all space. This subatomic Turing wave prediction now finds confirmation in recent nucleon scattering form factor data which show that the nucleon core has a Gaussian charge density distribution with a peripheral periodicity whose wavelength approximates the particle's Compton wavelength and which declines in amplitude with increasing radial distance. The subquantum kinetics explanation for the origin of charge correctly anticipates the observation that the proton's charge density wave pattern is positively biased while the neutron's is not. The phenomenon of beta decay is interpreted as the onset of a secondary bifurcation leading from the uncharged neutron solution to the charged proton solution. The Turing wave dissipative structure prediction is able to account in a unitary fashion for nuclear binding, particle diffraction, and electron orbital quantization. The wave packet model is shown to be fundamentally flawed implying that quantum mechanics does not realistically represent the microphysical world. This new conception points to the possible existence of orbital energy states below the Balmer ground state whose transitions may be tapped as a new source of energy.

title: EnergyAwakening
content_preview: A Paradigm Shift for a New Energy Awakening Paul A. LaViolette, Ph.D. The Starburst Foundation © June 24, 2007 Our preconceived notions of what is possible and what is impossible shape and limit our ability to make new discoveries and fashion new technologies. Let us begin with Newton's Third Law of Motion—for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. Put another way, this proposition forms the basis for the law of the conservation of momentum. Our physics books teach us that a body can only move forward in one direction by throwing mass off board in the opposite direction. This is how a rocket propels itself. But there are certain capacitor devices having asymmetrically disposed plates that are able to spontaneously move from an initial position of rest without expelling any mass; they do this merely by electrostatically charging their plates. One example is the Lafforgue field propulsion thruster. Electric field propulsion—violation of the conservation of momentum. title: Sympathetic Vibratory Physics
content_preview:
A self-taught mathematician working in a small Irish college quietly wrote a book in 1854 that would one day power every smartphone, laptop, and computer on earth. He had no idea.
George Boole was born in Lincoln, England in 1815 to a shoemaker father who couldn't afford a proper education for his son. So Boole educated himself, learning Latin, Greek, and advanced mathematics largely on his own.
He eventually landed a professorship at Queen's College Cork in Ireland, where he began pursuing one of the strangest questions in mathematics: could human reasoning itself be written as an equation?
The result was a system he called the algebra of logic. The core idea was that logical statements — things like "this is true" or "this is false" — could be expressed using symbols and manipulated mathematically, just like numbers in a standard equation.
Boole was not trying to build machines. He was doing philosophy with algebra, convinced that the laws of human thought could be expressed symbolically. His 1854 book, "An Investigation of the Laws of Thought," was a mathematical exploration of how the mind reasons and draws conclusions.
Bertrand Russell, one of the greatest mathematicians of the 20th century, later described that book as "the work in which pure mathematics was discovered."
Boole died in 1864 at just 49 years old, long before telephones, radio, or anything resembling an electronic machine existed. He never saw what his ideas would become.
Decades later, engineers discovered that electrical switches — which exist in only two states, on or off — could be wired together to perform the exact logical operations Boole had described on paper. His abstract system of true and false, yes and no, mapped perfectly onto the two physical states of any electronic circuit.
What Boole had called a philosophical investigation into the structure of thought became the operating language of every digital device ever built.

content_preview: European Journal of Applied Physics Vol 8 | Issue 5 | September 2026 ISSN 2684-4451 REVIEW Sustained Excess-Heat Production in Gas-Phase LENR Experiments Using Engineered Nanoscale Materials Steven B. Krivit1, * and Michael J. Ravnitzky2 ABSTRACT Reports in the low-energy nuclear reaction (LENR) literature describe observations of nuclear signatures and net energy production from hydrogen-fueled experiments. However, progress has been delayed by the lack of reproducible experimental pathways. In this review, we identify an emerging pathway involving low-energy input, gas-phase systems, and nanomaterials. Specifically, we review reports of (a) excess-heat production in which the output thermal power exceeds the total system input electrical power, (b) excess thermal power and time-integrated excess energy, (c) repeatability by originating research groups and reproducibility by independent laboratories, and (d) specific energy and energy density values that exceed known chemical energy-density limits under the reported normalization. Furthermore, we identify a shift in the last decade away from Pd–D2 electrolytic systems and toward more successful Ni–H2 gas-phase systems employing engineered nanoscale materials. We also discuss known unresolved technological challenges. LENR experiments are distinct from beam, accelerator, and other ion-driven fusion experiments as well as magnetic- and inertial-confinement fusion systems, which use moderate- to high-energy inputs to induce nuclear fusion reactions. The non-LENR approaches produce the expected fusion products. In contrast, LENR experiments involve materials-mediated condensed-matter processes initiated by much lower external input energies. LENRs produce nuclear reaction products, but they are not consistent with the product pairs, energies, and branching ratios expected from deuterium-deuterium (D-D) nuclear fusion.
